column2: Condition: H ≫ m₀, and m₀ is only of the order of decimetres (e.g. 0,6 m).
They dig down to m₀, place horizontal planks against the face, hold them with a vertical waling (1st generation) and strut it.
Another m₀ of deepening, more horizontal planks below. Next to the old ones, longer new walings (2nd) spanning the whole depth so far are placed; they are strutted, then the old ones are removed.
The same in the 3rd step: a new generation of walings, the old one comes out.
The 4th step – the length of the planks is not limited, and they are not damaged, since they are not driven.
With the 5th step we reach the final depth.
The shoring is complete. The method is slow and needs a lot of manual work – in return it is safe even with an m₀ of a few decimetres.
Condition: m₀ = 0 – coarse-grained soil, not even apparent cohesion: the face does not stand for a moment.
The vertical sheets – steel only – are driven or vibrated in before excavation.
Excavation of the first step under the protection of the sheets.
First row of walings and struts.
Excavation of the next step, another waling and strut.
Excavation to the final depth, third row of struts.
Complete: the ends of the sheets always remain at least 30 cm in the soil – so the soil cannot flow in below them.

Pre-excavation to about 1,0–1,25 m, over at most one box length. Meanwhile the box is assembled on the bank: two panels with adjustable struts between them.
The box is lowered into the pre-excavation with a four-leg chain.
Digging inside the box – at most 0,5 m below the edge of the panel.
The excavator pushes the box down corner by corner with the back of its bucket; the tilt of the struts may be at most 1:20.
Repeat. When the top of the basic box is about 20 cm above ground level, the extension is added.
At the final depth the edge of the box stands at least 10 cm above ground level. The gap between the box and the soil face is filled at once; ladder, edge protection.
Work in the box: the pipe is placed in the free space below the struts.
Moving on: the workers climb out, the box is lifted out and moved on – nobody may be inside while it is being moved. The finished section is backfilled in layers.
The trench is dug to full depth – this is only allowed in temporarily stable soil and over a short length.
The finished box is lowered into the trench.
The box is a passive shield: the soil moves until it rests on the panel – so the gap has to be filled at once. In loose soil and beside traffic this method is not allowed.
Pre-excavation to at most 1,25 m; the first panel and the rail frame are placed (two vertical steel rails with the roller carriage and its struts between them).
About 0,5 m of digging, then pushing down the rails.
Then pushing down the panels – alternately: no element may be more than 0,5 m ahead of the others.
Repeat to the final depth; the extension panel goes into the second guide groove of the rail.
The roller carriage can be set at any height: even a large-diameter pipe fits below it. With single / double / triple rails, to a depth of about 3,7 / 7,4 / 8,5 m (manufacturer’s data).
Longitudinal section along the axis of the trench: the dark part is the dug trench, in front of it the panel forming the box.
Digging below the edge of the panel
fill the gap – the box is only a shield!

Euler’s elastic critical force, strut pinned at both ends: Ncr = π²EI/L². Without safety factor, initial curvature and self-weight – illustrative. For timber the compressive strength (~20 MPa), for steel the yield strength (S355) gives the upper limit.

It buckles! A shorter strut, a larger cross-section or intermediate support is needed.
By Euler it still stands, but there is not enough reserve (about a threefold safety would be needed).
In an excavation wider than about 3 m a timber strut is already awkward – that is why bracing in several directions, raking struts or large-diameter steel tubes are needed.
Critical force – log scale (the horizontal part is the strength limit)
Resolution of forces: N = H / cos α, V = H · tan α (own calculation, illustrative). The vertical component of the raking strut lifts the wall and pushes the foot of the strut downwards.
The retaining wall stands, with the capping beam / waling on it. The middle of the excavation is dug out, but an earth berm is left beside the wall: its passive resistance holds the toe of the wall.
The inner part of the base slab is built, with steel brackets at its edge (or separate thrust blocks).
Raking struts are placed from the waling to the edge of the base slab; they are preloaded with a jack, then fixed with wedges.
The earth berm is removed in short, 5–7 m sections, alternately – never along the whole length at once.
In each excavated section the edge strip of the slab is concreted at once: from then on the slab supports the toe of the wall directly.
The strutting is only removed once the basement walls and slabs are complete and can take the earth pressure as diaphragms.
